stories.headline: Nvidia posts $96.2 billion quarter, more than double a year ago, and guides $108 billion next
stories.dek: Data Center $89.0 billion. Non-GAAP EPS $2.22. Gross margin 75%. China data-center compute assumed at zero in the guide.
stories.caveman: The AI chip giant finally printed. Second-quarter revenue hit $96.2 billion, up 106 percent from a year ago and above its own prior midpoint near $91 billion. Data Center alone did $89.0 billion. Adjusted earnings were $2.22 a share. Gross margin sat at 75 percent. For the next quarter Nvidia wants about $108 billion, plus or minus 2 percent, and it is not counting China data-center compute in that map. CEO Jensen Huang said compute is revenue now. Wall Street still has to decide if the beat was already priced in. The cash session had closed a touch lower before the release.
stories.why_it_matters: Nvidia sets the mood for every AI supply chain from Taiwan fabs to US utilities. A fat guide can lift Asian tech. A sold-the-news fade can erase a day of hope before Taipei even opens.
stories.camps: Bulls say demand is still supply-bound. Bears say the bar was already sky high. Factory workers feel the overtime, not the press-release adjectives.

terms.explain: What the company says next quarter's sales might be. Markets trade the guide as hard as the past quarter.
The big-server business that feeds AI training and inference. Most of Nvidia's sales live here.
Earnings after stripping some accounting items. Easier to compare, also easier to dress up.

stories.headline: US stocks barely budge into Nvidia: S&P 7,675, Nasdaq 26,130, Dow off 113 as PCE runs a touch hot
stories.dek: Core PCE matched forecasts at +0.2% month and +3.3% year. Investors waited for the after-bell chip print and Friday's Warsh speech.
stories.caveman: Wednesday's cash tape was a shrug. The S&P 500 slipped 0.02 percent to 7,675.70. The Nasdaq fell 0.08 percent to 26,130.20. The Dow lost 113 points. July core PCE rose 0.2 percent on the month and 3.3 percent on the year, right on the Dow Jones estimate; the headline PCE was a hair hotter than expected. Traders parked money until Nvidia spoke after the close and until Fed Chair Kevin Warsh speaks at Jackson Hole on Friday. The Philly semiconductor index actually rose 0.2 percent. Waiting is also a trade.
stories.why_it_matters: A flat US close into a mega-print means the real move may hit Asia first. Taiwan's Thursday open inherits both the earnings and the leftover inflation nerves.
stories.camps: Hawks say sticky services keep cuts distant. Doves say cooling spending gives the Fed room to sit. Renters feel the lag, not the decimal.

terms.explain: The Fed's favorite inflation gauge. Core skips food and energy noise.
A basket of chip stocks. It can rise even when the big indexes nap.
Company reports published once regular US trading ends. Futures then argue all night.

stories.headline: Oil eases again: WTI settles $82.23, Brent $87.84 as Hormuz diplomacy and new supply risks trade off
stories.dek: US crude down 13 cents. Brent down 74 cents. Third session of digestion after the prior week's sharp drop.
stories.caveman: Crude did not bounce hard. West Texas Intermediate settled at $82.23 a barrel, down 0.16 percent. Brent landed at $87.84, down 0.84 percent. Traders weighed talk of restoring Hormuz shipping against fresh supply risks from the wider Middle East and Ukraine wars. This is quieter than Tuesday's three-percent slide, but the direction still points down. Pump prices will lag the screen. They always do.
stories.why_it_matters: Cheaper barrels cool inflation talk and help risk assets. A sudden Hormuz scare can erase that cushion in hours.
stories.camps: Diplomacy bulls want corridors and minesweepers. Security hawks want stockpiles. Drivers still pay last week's fear.

terms.explain: The US oil sticker price.
The global oil sticker price set in London.
A narrow water gate for a huge share of seaborne oil. Tension there moves every barrel.

stories.image_alt: Oil market or energy trading imagery

stories.headline: Jackson Hole opens Thursday in Wyoming; Warsh's first Fed-chair keynote still lands Friday
stories.dek: Theme: financial innovation and payments. About 120 officials from 70-plus countries. Markets want rate clues more than panels.
stories.caveman: The mountain meeting is no longer a preview. Kansas City Fed opens Jackson Hole on Thursday, August 27, through Saturday. New Chair Kevin Warsh still gives the headline keynote Friday morning Eastern time. Official theme: financial innovation, payments, policy. Unofficial theme: will he sound hawkish after sticky inflation and a noisy Treasury market. No rate vote happens at the lodge. The speech can still reprice the dollar and Asian tech before Monday.
stories.why_it_matters: One careful paragraph from a new Fed chair can lift yields and knock growth stocks. Taiwan traders will hear him after their Friday open.
stories.camps: Hawks want proof he can stay tight. Doves want a path to easier money. Households want cheaper bread, not Wyoming scenery.

terms.explain: The annual mountain gathering where Fed chairs often sketch the next year of policy.
New US central-bank boss. Friday is his first big Jackson Hole speech as chair.
The talk everyone actually watches. Panels fill the rest of the schedule.

stories.headline: Meta agrees to an $18 billion deal with US states over social-media harms to children
stories.dek: Teen apps default to a two-hour daily cap, plus school and night modes. Part of the cash may hinge on TikTok and YouTube matching tougher limits.
stories.caveman: Meta settled a giant state case for about $18 billion. Forty-eight states and several territories signed on. The company will default under-18 users to a two-hour daily limit on Facebook and Instagram, add a night lock from midnight to 6 a.m., and quiet school-hour notifications unless parents override. A twist: Meta may pay only about 70 percent unless TikTok and YouTube also accept roughly one-hour teen defaults and help fund states. New Mexico and Florida stayed out after their own fights. Meta's stock popped on the news. Parents get tools. Critics say tools are not culture.
stories.why_it_matters: This is one of the largest platform liability checks yet. If the contingent claw works, teen time limits could spread beyond Meta by force of money.
stories.camps: Attorneys general call it accountability. Meta calls it closure. Teen users will find workarounds. Teachers want the school-mode hours to mean something.

terms.explain: A lawsuit ends with money and rule changes instead of a full trial.
The app starts with a time ceiling. Parents can loosen it, kids cannot quietly ignore it at first.
Notifications stay off during school hours so class is harder to interrupt.

stories.headline: Anthropic lines up about $45 billion in Vera Rubin compute from Britain's Nscale
stories.dek: Six-year rent deal tied to a West Virginia data center, capacity aimed at late 2027. Another chapter in the AI power shopping spree.
stories.caveman: Anthropic is buying time on other people's chips again. TechCrunch, citing a person familiar and Bloomberg, says the lab will rent roughly $45 billion of Nvidia Vera Rubin compute from Nscale, a young British infrastructure firm. The power is expected to come online late 2027 from Nscale's West Virginia flagship, over about six years. This follows other Anthropic checks: Volta in Norway, AMD, SpaceX capacity, Amazon gigawatts, Google and Broadcom. The pattern is simple. Labs that cannot build fabs buy warehouses of GPUs instead. Somebody still has to pay the power bill.
stories.why_it_matters: Compute leases this large lock in Nvidia demand and local electricity fights for years. They also raise the entry price for any smaller AI lab.
stories.camps: Anthropic says it needs fuel to compete. Critics say the industry is circular-financing a bubble. West Virginia residents will notice the substations first.

terms.explain: Nvidia's newer multi-chip AI system. Labs rent it in bulk before they can own enough.
Paying for future GPU hours, often measured in billions of dollars over years.
A 2024-founded British company selling big AI data-center capacity.

stories.headline: Apple sets Sept. 9 'Surprise and Shine' event as John Ternus prepares to take the CEO chair
stories.dek: Cook hands over Sept. 1. Rumors center on a foldable iPhone and iPhone 18 Pro models; standard iPhone 18 may wait.
stories.caveman: Apple put a date on the invite. September 9 at Apple Park, tagline Surprise and Shine. Tim Cook is due to hand the CEO job to John Ternus on September 1, so this is the first big stage for the new boss. Hardware whispers include a foldable iPhone plus iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max; the plain iPhone 18 may slip to next year. Watch Series 12, Ultra, and smart-home gear are also on the rumor board. For suppliers, the invite is a calendar. For fans, it is a trailer. For workers on assembly lines, it is overtime math.
stories.why_it_matters: Apple's event date starts a pricing and component countdown across Asia. A real foldable would reshuffle camera, hinge, and display winners.
stories.camps: Optimists want a category reboot. Skeptics expect Pro tweaks and a long demo. Repair shops already price folding screens in their nightmares.

terms.explain: Apple's headquarters theater for big product reveals.
A phone with a screen that bends. Long rumored, still unproven in Apple's hands.
The top boss changes. Markets listen harder to the first public script.

stories.headline: US says Chinese hackers hit Justice and NASA systems; domains seized as the investigation widens
stories.dek: Another reminder that AI headlines share the week with old-fashioned state cyber conflict.
stories.caveman: While chip earnings filled screens, security wires said Chinese hackers had broken into US Justice Department and NASA-related systems. Authorities said they seized linked domains. Details remain thin in early reports. The pattern is familiar: espionage against government and science networks, then a public takedown message. Companies shipping AI racks still run on the same internet that spies already map.
stories.why_it_matters: Cyber incidents against justice and space agencies raise insurance, compliance, and alliance costs even when markets obsess over GPUs.
stories.camps: US officials frame a state threat. Beijing usually denies. Security teams ask for patches, not geopolitics slogans.

terms.explain: Authorities take control of web addresses used in an attack or campaign.
A government-linked crew stealing data or access, not a random ransomware gang.
US civil space body. A breach there hits science and national prestige at once.

stories.headline: Trump says Hormuz mine-clearing is done and warns Iran against reseeding; Tehran still talks Oman corridor terms
stories.dek: Competing statements land in the same news cycle: US victory lap versus Iranian revenue-sharing talks with Oman.
stories.caveman: President Trump claimed the Strait of Hormuz has been cleared of mines and warned Iran that new mines would be answered by sinking. Iran, in parallel messaging, said it was still working with Oman on a temporary corridor and how to share related fees. Markets treated the mix as unfinished diplomacy, not a clean reopening. Oil slipped only a little. Shipping desks still want proof on the water, not podium lines.
stories.why_it_matters: Hormuz is a chokepoint for energy and food freight. Conflicting claims keep insurance high and delay any real freight relief.
stories.camps: Washington wants credit for force and clearance. Tehran wants leverage and fees. Ship captains want charts and escorts.

terms.explain: Removing sea mines so commercial ships can pass.
A limited shipping path agreed while a wider conflict continues.
Laying new mines after a clear. The threat that keeps insurers nervous.

stories.headline: Trump claims Iran's supreme leader is badly hurt on his left side; treat the battlefield boast as unverified
stories.dek: CNA carried the remark in early Thursday wires. Independent confirmation was not established in this morning window.
stories.caveman: Trump told audiences the war with Iran is nearing an end and that Iran's highest leader was severely injured on his left side. State media and wire picks moved the quote fast. Field Notes flags it as a claim, not a confirmed medical fact. Wars produce victory speeches before they produce evidence. Oil and Gulf aviation still price risk, not slogans.
stories.why_it_matters: Leader-casualty rumors can jolt markets and mislead civilians. Publishing the claim without a confirmation label would be reckless.
stories.camps: Trump allies sell an ending narrative. Iran denies or stays silent. Analysts wait for multiple sourcing.

terms.explain: The highest political-religious authority in Iran's system.
Something said in public that independent reporters have not proven yet.
Fast short dispatches other outlets reprint. Speed is not the same as proof.

stories.headline: Nepal-Tibet border floods and landslides kill scores; UN agencies report rising tolls in China and Nepal
stories.dek: Early tallies cited more than a hundred dead and hundreds missing across the Himalayan disaster zone.
stories.caveman: Monsoon water and mud hit the Nepal-China border hard. UN agencies on Wednesday described severe flooding with climbing death counts. Separate Taiwan and international wires spoke of a Tibet Gyirong landslide zone with multiple dead and hundreds missing, and of Nepal figures climbing past a hundred. Foreign tourists were among the missing in some reports. Rescue is racing weather. Exact totals will keep moving.
stories.why_it_matters: Climate-charged mountain disasters kill fast and cut trade roads. Aid lags because the same rain that kills also blocks trucks.
stories.camps: Governments promise relief. Locals want search teams now. Tour companies face refund and liability fights.

terms.explain: Hillsides of mud and rock that bury roads and villages after heavy rain.
The yearly wet season in South Asia. When it overperforms, valleys flood.
People not confirmed dead or found. In mountain disasters this number can stay high for days.

stories.headline: UN Security Council hears Gaza-West Bank briefing as settlement violence and fragile ceasefire strains persist
stories.dek: Special envoy puts human dignity at the center while attacks and settlement expansion continue in reporting.
stories.caveman: The Security Council met on the occupied Palestinian territory again. The UN special envoy said human dignity must sit at the center of efforts to hold a fragile ceasefire and ease suffering. Briefings pointed to continued Gaza and West Bank violence and settlement pressure. This is not a breakthrough story. It is the international system admitting the fire is still lit.
stories.why_it_matters: Without a durable ceasefire and aid access, famine and displacement metrics keep worsening even when markets look elsewhere.
stories.camps: Some states push accountability language. Others defend security operations. Civilians need corridors more than communiqués.

terms.explain: The UN body that can authorize sanctions or peace operations. It often deadlocks on Gaza.
Israeli civilian communities built in occupied territory. Expansion fuels legal and political fights.
A pause in fighting. Fragile means it can break with one strike.

stories.headline: IndieBound's new national list: Caro Claire Burke's Yesteryear holds No. 1 for week ending Aug. 26
stories.dek: The tradwife-to-1855 debut remains the Indies Introduce juggernaut after twenty weeks on the chart.
stories.caveman: Independent bookstores filed a fresh national list for the week ending August 26. Yesteryear by Caro Claire Burke is still No. 1 hardcover fiction. A modern tradwife influencer wakes in 1855 and must decide if the nightmare is a hoax, a show, or something worse. Twenty weeks on the list is not a fluke. Indies keep handselling it. That is how a debut outruns louder launches.
stories.why_it_matters: Indie charts show what readers buy when algorithms are quieter. A long-running No. 1 shapes fall book-club shelves.
stories.camps: Indie booksellers celebrate staying power. Big publishers chase the next shock premise. Readers just want the next chapter.

terms.explain: A bestseller list built from independent US bookstore sales.
A bookseller program that boosts promising new voices.
When bookstore workers personally recommend a title to customers.

stories.headline: Ann Patchett's Whistler and Kathryn Stockett's The Calamity Club pack the IndieBound top tier
stories.dek: Beloved names sit just under Yesteryear as summer softens into fall reading habits.
stories.caveman: Under the debut still ruling the chart, familiar heavyweights hold the next rungs. Ann Patchett's Whistler keeps drawing readers who want luminous, time-bending connection. Kathryn Stockett's The Calamity Club brings a big-hearted crew of women fighting for what is theirs. These are not obscure experiments. They are comfort-plus-craft titles that indies can sell to almost any adult browsing table.
stories.why_it_matters: When established literary brands share space with a debut, it signals a healthy mix of risk and trust at the register.
stories.camps: Patchett fans want another quiet masterpiece. Stockett readers want momentum and friendship. Critics argue about middlebrow power.

terms.explain: Ann Patchett's 2026 novel about sweetness, impermanence, and connection.
Kathryn Stockett's new big-canvas story of women and friendship.
The first few bestseller slots that get window space and club attention.

stories.headline: New on the indie chart: Sheila Masterson's The Poison Daughter arrives as a romantasy spike
stories.dek: A September Indie Next pick about deadly lips and the one man who can survive a kiss enters the national hardcover list.
stories.caveman: Romantasy still prints money. The Poison Daughter by Sheila Masterson shows up as new on the IndieBound hardcover fiction list. Pitch: a woman whose lips are poison meets the rare man who can live through her kiss. It is already a September Indie Next pick. Bookstores know the aisle. Enemies-to-lovers plus magic still converts browsers into buyers.
stories.why_it_matters: Chart newcomers reveal what indies think can interrupt the long-running leaders. Romantasy remains that interrupter.
stories.camps: Genre readers cheer another hit formula. Literary gatekeepers roll eyes. Teen and adult crossover shelves quietly expand.

terms.explain: Love story plus magic world. Currently one of publishing's strongest engines.
A monthly list of titles indie booksellers especially want to push.
First week a title appears on the bestseller ranking.

stories.headline: Paul Yoon's Etna and Chang-rae Lee's A Tender Age keep climbing regional and national indie conversations
stories.dek: A war-scarred working dog's odyssey and a child-of-immigrants masculinity novel show literary breadth beyond romantasy.
stories.caveman: Not every chart story is a kiss curse. Paul Yoon's Etna, the August Indie Next No. 1 in some regional tallies, follows a working dog after war trying to get home. Chang-rae Lee's A Tender Age watches American masculinity through a preteen immigrant child's confused eyes. Cool Machine, Colson Whitehead's 1980s Harlem entry, also holds. The point: indies are still balancing spectacle with quieter literary bets.
stories.why_it_matters: A healthy book culture needs more than one genre engine. These titles keep prize-and-seminar readers inside the same stores as romantasy fans.
stories.camps: Literary readers want Etna and Lee on tables. Sales floors want whatever turns fastest. Both can be true if stores keep diverse fronts.

terms.explain: Paul Yoon's novel about a working dog's postwar journey home.
A 2026 novel on family and masculinity through a child's eyes.
Stories sold on style and theme as much as plot hooks.

stories.headline: Armed attack in Kenscoff leaves bodies in Haitian streets; survivors search for missing relatives
stories.dek: Gunmen hit a farming community in the hills above Port-au-Prince late Sunday into Monday, burning homes.
stories.caveman: In Kenscoff, above Haiti's capital, armed men came at night. Houses burned. By Monday bodies lay in the streets and families hunted for the missing. UN photo and wire notes put the massacre in a country already hollowed by gangs. This is not abstract insecurity. It is a farming hill that woke up smaller.
stories.why_it_matters: When food-growing towns are torched, capital-city hunger rises next. Haiti's crisis keeps exporting displacement and importing despair.
stories.camps: Local leaders beg for security support. International actors argue about missions. Residents need safe roads before slogans.

terms.explain: A farming community overlooking Haiti's capital, hit in this attack.
Irregular armed crews that tax, burn, and displace civilians.
Leaving home because staying means death or extortion.

stories.headline: UN: 3.7 million Afghan children are wasted; about one million face the most life-threatening form
stories.dek: Fresh malnutrition stock-take lands while aid budgets stay thin. Wasting is the dangerous thinness that kills fast.
stories.caveman: New UN figures say some 3.7 million children in Afghanistan are wasted — dangerously thin for their height. About one million are in the most severe, life-threatening tier. This is a stock count of bodies, not a metaphor. Food, clinics, and cash assistance are all short. A child can look quiet and still be dying.
stories.why_it_matters: Malnutrition numbers this large mean an entire school generation is being medically scarred. Delayed aid becomes lifelong disability.
stories.camps: Aid agencies beg for funds. Donors cite fatigue and politics. Parents ration meals while arguing with no one who can hear.

terms.explain: A child is far too thin for their height. It can kill quickly without treatment.
The most dangerous malnutrition tier. Needs therapeutic food and medical care.
Money countries and charities set aside for emergency food and medicine.

stories.headline: UN desertification body names World Restoration Flagships as 40% of land faces degradation
stories.dek: Awards spotlight repair projects while drought already threatens livelihoods for more than three billion people.
stories.caveman: The UN Convention to Combat Desertification announced three World Restoration Flagship winners on Wednesday. The backdrop is brutal: about 40 percent of the world's land is degrading, and drought risks the livelihoods of more than three billion people. Awards do not water a field by themselves. They do mark places where repair is working well enough to copy.
stories.why_it_matters: Land loss is a quiet famine machine. Successful restoration models are scarce public goods.
stories.camps: Environmental agencies celebrate pilots. Farmers want subsidies and water rights. Finance ministries ask who pays at scale.

terms.explain: Land losing ability to grow food because of overuse, drought, or bad management.
Planting, resting, and rebuilding soil so farms and ecosystems can work again.
The UN treaty body focused on dryland and drought problems.

stories.headline: African health ministers back a decade plan as the continent faces a shortfall of over six million health workers by 2035
stories.dek: Addis Ababa meeting tries to grow the workforce before clinics empty out.
stories.caveman: Health ministers meeting in Addis Ababa heard a hard forecast: Africa could be short more than six million health professionals by 2035. They answered with a new decade-long workforce plan. Plans are paper. Training nurses and paying them enough to stay is the real fight. Without staff, vaccines and maternity wards are just buildings.
stories.why_it_matters: A worker gap this size turns every future epidemic and every childbirth into a worse lottery.
stories.camps: Ministers promise investment. Young clinicians still migrate for pay. Patients notice wait times before they notice strategy docs.

terms.explain: The people who actually deliver care. Buildings without them are empty.
Host city for the health ministers' meeting.
Trained staff leaving for better pay abroad, emptying home clinics.
